worthwhile_why: The reassuring answer ('editing main does NOT fragilely restart the daemon mid-work') depends on stored mechanism knowledge of the daemon's lifecycle — specifically that the staleness/fingerprint check fires only at SessionStart while per-turn hooks just ping a persistent process. That is not derivable from the conversation in front of it (the prior turns covered only the worktree-mismatch case).
needed_knowledge: The brain daemon is a persistent process that loads Python modules once at startup; edits to servers/*.py are NOT hot-reloaded — a running daemon keeps serving the old code until it is restarted. (Foundation for 'edit main, keep working, daemon keeps running old code untouched.')

The staleness/fingerprint check (ensure_daemon + _code_changed) runs only at SessionStart (boot-brain.sh); per-turn hooks (recall, pre-edit, stop) just ping the already-running daemon via daemon_call_raw and never recompute the fingerprint. So the restart cadence is once per new session, not per edit.

On main the boot-time refresh converges in a single restart because the daemon boots from main = exactly the code that was edited; recovery-driven restarts fire only when the daemon is unreachable. This is 'pick up new code next session,' not fragility.

Without it the answer is hand-derived; with it the persistence-and-converge claim is grounded.

encode_gaps: The precise trigger map the outcome delivers: per-turn hooks (recall/pre-edit/stop) call daemon_call_raw and ONLY ping the running daemon — they never recompute the code fingerprint; ensure_daemon + _code_changed runs only at SessionStart, and recovery (ensure_daemon) restarts only when the daemon is unreachable. No node states this boot-vs-per-turn timing distinction — the model had to derive it by reading the code live. (Existing nodes capture 'daemon is persistent, restart to pick up code' but not WHICH events recompute the fingerprint, which is exactly the answer to 'is the daemon fragilely restarting during work on main?')
